title: Build Something That Outlives You
author: Michael Foster
summary: A bivocational pastor uses a viral video critiquing personal brands to develop a distinction between being a "person of influence" and being an "influencer," and applies it directly to pastoral leadership and church succession. Influence, he argues, is built slowly through local, accountable, real-world work and survives the platform that carried it; an influencer's audience has weak real-world ties, rewards novelty and flattery, and creates "key man risk" where an institution's health becomes hostage to one person's continued visibility. He recounts a church where attendance dropped 30% whenever the senior pastor wasn't preaching, and another where a founder's brass statue made succession nearly impossible, as cautionary examples. The essay's organizing concept is "self-liquidating leadership" -- a pastor's job is to make himself increasingly unnecessary by raising up other leaders and directing attention toward the institution rather than himself, so the measure of good leadership is what survives after the leader is gone.
points: Foster's central distinction is that influence is built slowly through local, accountable, real-world relationships, while an influencer's power rests on a weakly-tied audience that rewards novelty and punishes confrontation.

He names "key man risk" as the structural danger of personality-driven institutions: one church saw attendance drop roughly 30% whenever the senior pastor wasn't the one preaching, proof the congregation's health had become entangled with one man's visibility.

The organizing concept of "self-liquidating leadership" reframes a leader's job as making himself increasingly unnecessary -- raising up successors and directing credit outward rather than consolidating it.

Foster argues buzz and attention can actively mask institutional weakness, so the right diagnostic question for an organization's health is not how influential its leader is but whether he is building something that survives his departure.
quotes: Influence is something that's built over time, that's tied to real-world accomplishments, like building an institution, whether it's a church or a family. And consequently, influence is something that gathers slowly and has strong ties locally.

A person of influence, because their influence emanates from a local reality, is generally answerable to people who can actually confront them, which is quite different from an influencer whose accountability is derived from metrics such as audience capture and engagement.

Lawrence points out that with personal brands, the influencer becomes the marketing. This results in something that's called key man risk. The growth and morale of the congregation end up being substantially dependent on that one man's presence.

I remember a pastor on staff telling me that they had to conceal whether or not the senior pastor was preaching on a given Sunday because they would see a massive drop in attendance, something like 30%.

It's foolish to measure the health of your church by how influential your pastor is. Really, from an organizational standpoint, what you should be asking is: Is he increasingly making himself unnecessary?
The greatest measure of whether or not you built well is what happens after you are no longer there to hold it together.
